author: historian-agent:gemini-flash-outline
title: Phoenician city-states and trading network
summary: Phoenician city-states on the Levantine coast, led by Tyre and Sidon, thrived as traders and manufacturers from about 1500 BCE and, from around 1100 BCE, spread colonies across the Mediterranean, among them Gades (Cadiz) and Carthage. They were famed for ships, glass and the purple dye of Tyre. Their alphabet, carried to Greece, underlies most Western scripts written today. Alexander the Great's conquest of Sidon and Tyre in 332 BCE ended the independence of the homeland cities.

uncertainty.note: Extensive maritime trade and colonization developed c. 1100 BCE (astronomical -1099); core Levantine city-states were incorporated into Hellenistic empires after Alexander's siege of Tyre in 332 BCE (astronomical -331), while western colonies like Carthage survived until 146 BCE (astronomical -145).

as_recorded.value: founded prosperous colonies such as Cadiz and Carthage

where.historical_name: Tyre (Ṣūr), Phoenician island city-state and maritime commercial hub

importance.justification: Linked the Mediterranean by sea, founded Carthage and spread the alphabet, which has its own record (R3 D2 T4 L3).

related.because: WHE says the Phoenician alphabet, carried to Greece, is the basis of most Western scripts.
